details:
**Binding of Isaac on Mount Moriah (the Akedah)**
God tests Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice his son Isaac on Mount Moriah; Abraham binds the boy on an altar, but an angel stops him and a ram caught in a thicket is offered instead. God then promises to multiply his descendants "as the stars in the heavens and as the sand on the shores of the sea." Jewish tradition calls this the Akedah ("binding"), and Abraham answers God's call with "Hineini" ("Here I am").

**Eid al-Adha and Qurbani**
The Islamic "Festival of the Sacrifice" commemorates Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son, whom Muslims usually identify as Ishmael (Isma'il) rather than Isaac. Muslims perform Qurbani, the slaughter of an animal, in his honor, and pilgrims on Hajj perform the Stoning of the Devil at three pillars, recalling Ibrahim driving away Shaitan when he tempted him to disobey God.

**Builder of the Kaaba**
In Islamic tradition, Ibrahim and his son Ishmael built (or rebuilt) the Kaaba in Mecca, the cube-shaped shrine Muslims face in prayer, and the angel Jibreel brought him the Black Stone set in its corner. The Maqam Ibrahim, a stone near the Kaaba kept in a gilded enclosure, is believed to bear his footprints, and he is credited with establishing the rites of Hajj.

**Hagar (Hajar) and Ishmael; Safa and Marwa; Zamzam**
Abraham fathered his firstborn Ishmael with Hagar, the Egyptian handmaid of his wife Sarah, and later sent mother and son away at Sarah's insistence after Isaac's birth. In Islamic tradition Hajar ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa seeking water until God made the Zamzam well spring up near the crying infant; Hajj pilgrims re-enact her run, and Ishmael became the ancestor of the Arabs and of Muhammad.

**Thrown into Nimrod's fire**
In the Quran and Jewish midrash, the tyrant king Nimrod (Namrud) has Ibrahim thrown (in some versions catapulted) into a great fire for rejecting idols. God commands the fire to be "cool" and "peaceful" for him, and in some tellings it burns only his chains, so he walks out unharmed.

**"Make the sun rise from the West"**
In Surah al-Baqarah, Ibrahim debates Nimrod about God's power. When Nimrod claims he too can give life and death, Ibrahim says that God brings the sun from the East and challenges the king to make it rise from the West, leaving him dumbfounded. In later legend, Nimrod is then destroyed by an army of gnats.

**Smashing his father's idols (Azar / Terah)**
The Quran names his father Azar; Genesis names him Terah, an idol maker or idol seller in Ur. In a famous midrash, the young Abraham smashes every idol in the shop except the largest, hangs his axe on it, and says the big idol did it, exposing that idols are powerless. This rejection of idolatry earns him the Islamic epithet hanif (a pure monotheist before Islam, opposed to the pagan Jahiliyyah) and the title Khalilullah, "Friend of God."

**Bargaining for Sodom: ten righteous men**
In Genesis 18, Abraham pleads with God to spare Sodom and Gomorrah, haggling the number of righteous people needed down from fifty to ten. Ten cannot be found, so the cities are destroyed, though his nephew Lot and Lot's daughters escape.

**Claiming his wife was his sister**
Twice Abraham passes off his wife Sarah as his sister to protect himself: first before the Pharaoh of Egypt, and later before Abimelech, king of Gerar, who takes her into his house. Abimelech returns her after a divine warning and gives Abraham a thousand pieces of silver; Abraham later swears an oath with Abimelech at Beersheba and plants a tamarisk tree there.

**Battle of the Vale of Siddim and Melchizedek**
When King Chedorlaomer and his allies capture Lot, Abraham leads 318 trained men to rescue him. Afterward Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem, brings out bread and wine and blesses him, and Abraham gives him a tenth of the spoils; Hebrews 7 uses this tithe to argue that Christ's priesthood "after the order of Melchisedec" is superior to the Levitical priesthood.

**Cave of Machpelah (Cave of the Patriarchs)**
Abraham buys this cave in Hebron from Ephron the Hittite to bury Sarah, and he is later buried there himself. It becomes the tomb of the patriarchs and matriarchs, and after Sarah's death Abraham fathers more children, including Midian, with Keturah.

**Three visitors and Sarah's laughter**
At the oaks of Mamre, Abraham hosts three strangers, later revealed as angels, and serves them a meal of meat and dairy. They announce that the elderly Sarah, about ninety, will bear a son; she laughs, and the boy is named Isaac (Yitzhak, "he laughs"). Christians often read this scene as a foreshadowing of the Trinity, and in the Quranic version the guests refuse to eat.

**Covenant: from Abram to Abraham**
God calls Abram out of his homeland to Canaan in the Torah portion "Lech Lecha" ("Go forth"), and he builds an altar at Shechem where the land is promised to his offspring. In the covenant of Genesis 17, his name changes from Abram to Abraham ("father of many nations"), Sarai becomes Sarah, and Abraham circumcises himself at age 99.

**Four birds on four hills**
In Surah al-Baqarah, when Ibrahim asks God to show him how He raises the dead, God tells him to cut up four birds and place their pieces on separate hills. When Ibrahim calls them, the birds come back to life and fly to him.

**Faith "counted to him as righteousness"**
Genesis 15:6, which says Abraham "believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness," is quoted three times in the New Testament, notably in Romans 4, where Paul notes that Abraham saw his own body "as good as dead" yet trusted God's promise of an heir. Hebrews 11 praises him for leaving home "not knowing where he was going," and in John 8 Jesus tells the Pharisees, "Before Abraham was, I am."
